verification.note: Institutional account read: connects Duby’s 1970 inaugural method with Bloch and Febvre and differentiates aristocracies, warfare, economic psychology, imaginaries, kinship and marriage. Supports a situated methodological relation, not exclusive affiliation or direct reading of the original lectures.

existing_sources_reused.title: Georges Duby, The Three Orders: Feudal Society Imagined, translated by Arthur Goldhammer (Chicago, 1980); French original 1978.
existing_sources_reused.citation: Georges Duby, The Three Orders: Feudal Society Imagined, translated by Arthur Goldhammer (Chicago, 1980); French original 1978.

verification.note: Publisher description reproduced by Google Books and contents read. The three orders are an imagined hierarchy connected with political/social conditions, not a literal census of medieval occupations. French 1978 bibliographic date checked in Wiley French Historians 1900–2000 chapter record https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/9781444323658.ch13 . Full book unread. The description contains a suspect seventh-century wording; that chronology is not used.

existing_sources_reused.title: Institut de France, “L’histoire des femmes en Occident,” interview presentation for Michelle Perrot, 6 March 2009.
existing_sources_reused.citation: Institut de France, “L’histoire des femmes en Occident,” interview presentation for Michelle Perrot, 6 March 2009.

verification.note: Written interview presentation and bibliography read; audio not listened to. Identifies Duby/Perrot’s five-volume 1991–1992 co-directed project and qualifies Annales’ earlier openings toward women’s history as limited. Supports collaboration and its scope, not every assertion in the presentation about women’s literacy/work or an Annales origin for feminist history. Volumes unread.

existing_sources_reused.citation: Lawrence Stone, “The Revival of Narrative: Reflections on a New Old History,” Past & Present 85 (1979): 3–24.

verification.note: Primary PDF read: printed 3–6 and 13–24 complete; 7–12 unread. Page 3 visually inspected, 5 and 13–23 OCR recovered because embedded text clips lines; 4, 6 and 24 read embedded text. Includes all notes on these pages, not all article notes. Starn directs Stone to White; examples and methodological limits are explicit. Broad historiographical diagnoses, dismissive descriptions and implied psychologies remain Stone’s claims. Montaillou citation 1976 is not adopted as first publication; quoted Elias reception/edition shorthand not certified. Prior Oxford metadata retained; book bodies not thereby read.

reading_limit: Existing bounded readings by Verdure, Stone and Hobsbawm remain named and qualified. Duby’s complete books and original inaugural lecture are not newly read. Histoire des femmes remains co-directed with Michelle Perrot and 1991–1992; other contributors’ chapters are not reassigned. No blanket narrative turn, sole authorship or continuous career interval.

relations.relationship: Provides a case for debating the relation between narrative presentation and historical analysis through Le Dimanche de Bouvines.
relations.evidence_note: Named substantive readers: Stone 1979, read pp. 3–6 and 13–24 only, and Hobsbawm’s complete 1980 response. Duby’s book itself remains unread. This records the use of his work in the debate, not his acceptance of Stone’s entire historiographical diagnosis.
